entries.abstract: Decomposition methods extrapolate the observed relationship between an outcome and an explanatory variable and are often used for counterfactual predictions in non-strategic settings. When the outcome arises from a game where agents gain by deviating from their strategies after a new policy, such predictions, though practically simple, are hard to justify. Our main result provides formal conditions in Bayesian games under which decomposition-based predictions coincide with equilibrium-based ones. This follows from an invariance condition on equilibrium selection rules, automatically satisfied in games with a unique equilibrium. We illustrate by revisiting Ciliberto and Tamer (2009)'s empirical analysis of airline entry decisions.
entries.title: A Decomposition Approach to Counterfactual Analysis in Game-Theoretic Models

entries.abstract: We demonstrate that a general-purpose coding agent can directly drive a physical robot throughout task execution without any task-specific or environment-specific training. We introduce Agent as Policy (AGP), which places task planning and execution under the agent's control. Given a task and a robot interface, the agent interprets visual evidence, writes executable programs, issues motion commands, and revises its actions in response to physical outcomes. This brings the agent's reasoning and programming capabilities into continuous interaction with the physical world. We study AGP across multiple real-world manipulation tasks spanning precision manipulation, dynamic motions, and deformable objects. These include assembly from human videos, block construction from goal images, dice flipping, targeted throwing, and bimanual towel folding. AGP achieves success rates of at least 80% in seven of eight task configurations and significantly outperforms previous agentic robot systems. We further study efficiency through task experience accumulation and find that reusing saved procedures and programs shortens execution time across repeated trials. These findings support a path for general-purpose agents to act as robot policies, extending their autonomy to physical manipulation through runtime reasoning, programming, and interaction.
entries.title: Agent as Policy for Robotic Manipulation

entries.abstract: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities. Each player observes a single conditionally independent signal and then repeatedly takes publicly observed actions to maximize their expected discounted payoff, which depends only on the state and their own action. We show that, when there are sufficiently many players and they are sufficiently patient, there exist equilibria where information is aggregated: the players' payoffs approximate the full-information payoff. This holds even if actions are uninformative under myopic play. Conversely, even if myopic play reveals the state, there also exist equilibria where information is not aggregated: payoffs approximate those under autarky. Our results speak to the range of possible outcomes of social learning games with forward-looking agents.
entries.title: Folk Theorems for Social Learning

entries.abstract: The complexity of navigating digital privacy, safety, and security threats often falls directly on users. This leads to users seeking help from family and peers, platforms and advice guides, dedicated communities, and even large language models (LLMs). As a precursor to improving resources across this ecosystem, our community needs to understand what help seeking looks like in the wild. To that end, we build a scaled analysis pipeline leveraging LLMs to sift through over two billion Reddit posts from the last five years to identify where and for what users seek digital privacy, safety, or security help. We isolate four million relevant posts with 93% precision and recall and automatically annotate each with the topics discussed (e.g., privacy configurations, data misuse, account compromise, and more). We use this dataset to understand the scope and scale of help seeking on Reddit, the subcommunities that provide help, and to qualitatively analyze the types of help sought. Our work informs the development of better resources for users (e.g., user guides or LLM help-giving agents) while underscoring the inherent challenges of supporting users through complex combinations of threats, platforms, mitigations, context, and emotions.
entries.title: Understanding Help Seeking for Digital Privacy, Safety, and Security on Reddit

entries.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.
entries.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights

entries.abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
entries.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark

entries.abstract: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
entries.title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems

entries.abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks. We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.
entries.title: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents

entries.abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular SKILL.md skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.
entries.title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory for Graphic Design Agent

entries.abstract: People's opinions can change both from their interactions with each other and from their interactions with media sources. Bounded-confidence models (BCMs) of opinion dynamics provide one framework to study such dynamics. In a BCM, the nodes of a network are agents with continuous-valued opinions, and these agents interact with each other via the edges of the network. In this paper, we extend the original Deffuant--Weisbuch (DW) BCM by incorporating influence from two media sources --- one with a positive value and one with a negative value --- to capture the effects of a polarized media landscape. We show both numerically and analytically that our extended DW model exhibits drifting behavior in which a large cluster of opinions shifts toward one of the media agents. We analyze how the drift trajectory and speed depend on the model parameters, and we identify conditions in which drift is promoted or suppressed. Our results provide insight into how competing media sources can influence collective opinion formation in social systems.
entries.comment: 24 pages; revised version; one new numerical experiment and associated figure; some revised discussions
entries.title: Drift Behavior in a Bounded-Confidence Opinion Model with Media Influence

entries.abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.
entries.title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction

entries.abstract: Datalog underpins reasoning tasks such as program analysis, but its programs are hard to write. Existing synthesizers automate this task but require users to state their intent as input-output examples. Large language models (LLMs) suggest a more natural route, text-to-Datalog synthesis from a natural-language question, yet how well they do so has not been systematically evaluated. We present DatalogBench, a benchmark of 136 text-to-Datalog synthesis tasks curated from existing Datalog-based artifacts. Synthesized programs are graded by execution on held-out inputs against an oracle validated by mutation analysis. Across six LLMs and four prompting configurations, exact match peaks at 75.7%; an input-output example raises it by about six points, while relation descriptions add little. Under direct prompting, most failures occur at compile time, typically because a model invents auxiliary predicates that it never declares or types consistently. Two coding agents reach up to 86.8% and eliminate nearly all such failures, leaving mostly semantic errors concentrated in recursive tasks. DatalogBench thus identifies recursive reasoning and decomposition as open challenges for current LLMs and agents, and offers a reliable, execution-grounded measure of both.
entries.title: DatalogBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Text-to-Datalog Synthesis

entries.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.
entries.title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

entries.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $κ= 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.
entries.title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks

entries.abstract: How closely does machine transcription agree with manual double-entry data? We digitize the 1912 and 1921 editions of the American Medical Directory, a national register of US physicians with roughly 140,000 and 150,000 entries in the two volumes, and compare five machine-extraction workflows with a full-count double-entered manual transcription. Like many historical directories, the AMD is semi-structured rather than tabular, so errors arise from misreading the layout as well as the text. A script that parses commercial OCR text using rules written by coding agents recovers about 97 percent of manually transcribed records with similar precision, more than a multimodal language model workflow (gemini-2.0.flash) that reads the page images and the OCR text. When the two methods fail, they fail on partly overlapping sets of records, so reconciling their outputs raises both recall and precision to about 98 percent. An open-weight LLM pipeline run on a local GPU server falls between the parser and the multimodal workflow in recall, and replacing the commercial OCR model with an open-source alternative lowers its recall by only about 2 percentage points. As the manual transcription's own error rate is unknown, these rates measure agreement rather than accuracy. Direct processing charges for the commercial OCR and multimodal workflow were about 0.03 euro per page, compared with 14.70 euro per page for manual transcription.
entries.title: The American Medical Directory Panel: Comparing AI-Assisted and LLM Transcription with Manual Data Entry at Scale

entries.abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.
entries.title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration

entries.abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, yet evaluations rarely report whether a measurement actually fits the trace it describes. We study what happens when those measurements do not fully capture the trace's behavior. Agents solve GSM8K problems with a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, which gives ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported; a chemistry task with search and retrieval tests the case where the model cannot recompute the tool's output. Across eight models and up to 1,000 traces per model, final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation disagree in systematic ways. The most common gap is the silent tool-output override: the model replaces a corrupted value without calling the tool again, so the error stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review finds verification labels the least reliable (\k{appa} =0.29), and checking depends on the task: the same calculator that several models re-checked on arithmetic was never re-checked on chemistry. Execution limits and serving failures also change what is measured. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should be reported with its evidence, whether the detector's question applied, whether the run was censored, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.
entries.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation

entries.abstract: Artificial intelligence in the Earth sciences is beginning to act: prototype agents already search archives, run simulations and draft analyses. Scientific data were curated for researchers who bring expert judgement; an autonomous agent cannot be assumed to supply it. Data can satisfy the FAIR principles and still mislead a machine acting alone. We propose that Earth-science data become AWARE (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled), an agent-specific requirements layer that extends FAIR, within a three-part agenda: AWARE data, bounded tools, layered validation. The ingredients exist across community infrastructure. We outline a staged, measurable path to adoption, intended to reduce silent error.
entries.comment: 34 pages (27 main text, 7 Supplementary Information), 1 figure, 1 table, 2 boxes
entries.title: From FAIR to AWARE: Data Readiness for Agentic AI in the Earth Sciences
Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

entries.abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models likely outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification), while weaker models score near or below them. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.
entries.title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research

entries.abstract: Good news about a strategy need not translate into evolutionary success. We study how the interaction between information and strategy exposure shapes evolutionary dynamics and equilibrium predictions. We derive the associated population dynamic from a simple revision process in which agents encounter candidate strategies at state-dependent rates and adopt them after receiving favorable payoff signals. We distinguish the monotone likelihood ratio property (MLRP) of signals from effective MLRP, which accounts for exposure relative to population shares and determines whether better-performing strategies grow faster. Random population encounters preserve MLRP and generate payoff-monotone evolution. When exposure sufficiently favors rare strategies, effective MLRP is violated near strict pure Nash equilibria, rendering them unstable. Conversely, when exposure sufficiently favors popular strategies, effective MLRP is violated near non-Nash pure states, allowing them to remain locally stable. Thus, even when signals satisfy MLRP, differences in strategy exposure can reverse their evolutionary implications and alter equilibrium predictions.
entries.title: When Good News Fails in Evolution: A Note on Information, Exposure, and Evolutionary Stability

entries.abstract: As voice agents gain more popularity commercially, the user simulators used to evaluate the deployed agents are also being developed to include more realistic, variable, and diverse speech naturalness behaviors -- disfluency, interruption and backchanneling. The quality of the user simulator directly affects the validity of agent evaluation results. However, we find that most studies so far have not examined in detail whether the intended configuration for these behaviors is realized in the simulation. In this study, we audit the realized naturalness behaviors of tau-Voice, our own LLM-based prompting approach across three models, and our rule-based injection algorithm for disfluency, interruption, and backchanneling. We find that prompting for these behaviors is unreliable and produces speech inconsistent with the instructions, placed and distributed less naturally than the instruction implies. In contrast, our rule-based, model-free algorithm produces controllable and diverse naturalness behaviors more aligned with natural speech. Our results suggest that LLMs not purpose-trained for user simulation are not sufficient on their own to represent authentic user behavior, and that linguistically informed deterministic approaches or specialized models are needed to close the gap; auditing and reporting realized naturalness behaviors, rather than configured settings, is what makes that gap visible.
entries.comment: Accepted to the UserSim @ NeurIPS 2026 workshop (non-archival)
entries.title: Prompts versus Rules: Auditing and Controlling Speech Naturalness Behaviors in Voice User Simulators

entries.abstract: Nonreciprocal interactions can break detailed balance by sustaining stationary probability currents. We ask whether such currents can also emerge when agents' immediate coordination preferences are reciprocal but their adjustment rules result from forward-looking optimization. We study a minimal stochastic linear--quadratic game in which two agents control noisy scalar states and minimize individual discounted costs in a full-information feedback Nash equilibrium. The optimized controls yield an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process whose stationary current, entropy production, and inter-agent information flow follow exactly from the Nash feedback. For reciprocal coordination with unequal self-anchoring, the drift asymmetry first appears at order $τ^5$, where $τ$ is the planning timescale, and the normalized entropy production scales as $τ^8$. We trace this delay to one mechanism: the asymmetry is set by the mismatch between the agents' value-function curvatures along the coordinate each does not control. At leading order this equals the mismatch of the corresponding cost curvatures, which instantaneous incentives cannot see and which the coordination cost fixes to zero; unequal persistence of the partners' fluctuations generates a value-function mismatch at order $τ^3$, postponing the asymmetry to fifth order, while a direct stake in the partner's state restores a cubic law. The normalized information flow, of order $τ^4$, identifies the weakly anchored agent as the one that tracks its partner. For conformist--contrarian coupling, normalized entropy production starts from a nonzero limit and initially decreases as $τ^2$; for equal anchoring, we prove that its long-foresight limit lies below the short-foresight value and that the stationary mutual-information flow vanishes. Numerical solutions of the full Nash equations confirm these laws.
entries.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures. Numerical code available at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24351245
entries.title: Foresight-dependent entropy production in stochastic two-agent dynamics

entries.abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.
entries.comment: This paper subsumes arXiv:2603.16744. 45 pages, including appendices
entries.title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research

entries.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 10 main content pages, 3 figures, L4DC submission
entries.title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger

entries.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, the standard injection template (AgentDojo's important_instructions) never redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY. Across 12 AgentDojo cells, SPILLWAY leads tested defenses in mean under-attack utility and composite scores. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, mean attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker stays below one percent, and SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

entries.abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

entries.title: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning

entries.abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.
entries.title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments

entries.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

entries.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions

# v0.34.0 **1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new).** Thank you! ## TL;DR - **10 new models** (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!) - **Extensible KV cache is on by default:** vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now **remove `gpu_memory_utilization`** from your configs. - **Model Runner V1 is gone.** Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner. - **Big speedups** on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3). - **Upgrade check:** default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` is required. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade). ## Before you upgrade > [!IMPORTANT] > These changes can break existing setups. | Change | What to do | PR | |---|---|---| | Model Runner V1 removed | Remove `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor`. | #63373 | | Default `--block-size` is 64 (was 16) | Pass `--block-size 16` to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. | #63231 | | Extensible KV cache on by default; `gpu_memory_utilization` defaults to 1.0 | **In most cases it's now best to not set `gpu_memory_utilization`**. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. | #56492 | | ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped | Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. `-rocm72` is no longer published. | #61939 | | `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` required | Also requires `tokenizers >= 0.23.3` and `timm >= 1.0.30`. | #64779 | | QuTLASS / `fp_quant` removed | `fp_quant` checkpoints no longer load. | #65230 | | Marlin W4A8 removed | Use `--quantization humming` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` instead of `VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE`. | #65542 | | Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed | — | #64287 | All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in [the full changelog](#full-changelog). ## New models | Model | Notes | PR | |---|---|---| | **Mistral Large 4** | 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. | #64534 | | MiniMax-M3.1-Flash | Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft | #64111 | | NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe | 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and `/v1/audio/transcriptions` | #64282 | | Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview | BF16 and NVFP4, `ripple` reasoning and tool parsers | #65745 | | Zyphra ZAYA1 | ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview | #65302 | | Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 | DASH sparse attention | #64016 | | Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio | | #65826, #65827, #65828 | | NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 | ASR and X↔En translation | #64215 | | Ming3-ASR | | #63585 | | NVIDIA Parakeet TDT | Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin | #65005 | ## Highlights ### Extensible KV cache, on by default - On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free **after** CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492). - **Result:** a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency. - **Trade-off:** per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` or `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache`. - Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674). ### Model Runner V2 only - Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373). - Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464). ### Speculative decoding - **Suffix decoding** runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339). - **Custom speculators:** declarative configs plus a `register_speculative_method` plugin API (#63205). - **CUDA graphs** for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989). - **Adaptive verification** works with XPress (#65175). - **Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype**, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198). ### Performance | Improvement | Hardware | Gain | PR | |---|---|---|---| | Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen | 4×GB200 | up to **1.95×** decode | #65152 | | GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE | NVIDIA | **1.6×** output throughput vs DEP4 | #60895 | | Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.5×** single-stream decode | #64077 | | Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) | GB200 | GLM-5.3 TTFT **1.24–1.40×** faster at 32K–128K | #63956 | | KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.34–1.59×** decode attention | #63638 | | Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) | NVIDIA | **3.0–8.8%** lower decode ITL | #51012 | | FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark | 8×MI355X | **+35–57%** interactivity at conc. 1–8 | #63440 | ### AMD ROCm - Release images and wheels are **ROCm 10.0 only** (#61939). - MoRI EPv2 via `--all2all-backend mori` (#61361). - Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435). - TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418). ### Serving and operations - **Checkpoint/restore** (CRIU + `cuda-checkpoint`) through `/checkpoint/prepare`, `/checkpoint/status` and `/checkpoint/restore`, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570). - **Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down:** dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370). - Best-effort **NUMA binding** on by default (#61258). - Opt-in **cache-aware admission** ordering (#54625). - Rust frontend: stateless **Responses API** (#63902) and **`n > 1`** (#65625). ## Install **Python wheels** | Platform | Install | |---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) | `pip install vllm` | | CUDA 13.0 (uv) | `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto` | | ROCm 10.0 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100` | | XPU | `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match` | **Docker images** | Platform | Image | Short alias | |---|---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (default) | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0` | | CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa` | | ROCm 10.0 | `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm` | | CPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu` | | XPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu` | `latest` tags work the same way (e.g. `vllm/vllm:latest-rocm`). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The `-efa` image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576). The **Assets** section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels. ## Full changelog

faster DCP sparse-indexer top-k (#65178, #64129). - Cross-layer KV cache sharing for MLA layers (#64095). - Fixes: PP rank derivation under PCP (#65539), FlashInfer MLA DCP decode (#59392). - **KV connectors** - NIXL: push mode via `transfer_mode` (#64230); `ucx_backend_params` (rocm_ipc on MI355X: 3.4 → 483.7 Gbps, #62905); 38% fewer hybrid SSM transfer bytes (#62317); block pairing across different P/D block sizes (#59746), with mismatched push handshakes rejected (#59747); no zero-filled pool (#64345). - KVCR v0.2.0 (#64224, #63889); async lookups published per request group (#57474); secondary tiers rejected on multi-node engines (#62930). - Hardened P2P tier (#63781, #64250, #64256, #64251, #64501, #63618, #64300, #63988) and correctness fixes (#64229, #63566, #65279, #65631, #64400, #63937, #65640). - **HiSparse** - Uses the extensible KV cache by default: 16% more GPU+host KV capacity (#65214). - Fused slot invalidation, up to 1.8% lower TPOT on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 (#60103); API and frontend - **New endpoints and options** - `/checkpoint/prepare`, `/checkpoint/status`, `/checkpoint/restore` (#62570). - `thinking_token_budget` on `/v1/responses` (#63896); `/v1/completions` in `vllm run-batch` (#64097). - Streaming derender on `/inference/v1/generate` (#63103). - Anthropic Messages API: `min_tokens` (#65459) and `thinking.type=between_tools` (#65954). - `vllm:request_render_duration_seconds` histogram (#60213). - **Tool calling and reasoning** - New `granite_toolcall_parser` for Granite 4.2 (#65216); llama3_json moved to the ParserEngine (#63569). - Incremental streaming for Kimi K3 (#62203), `tool_choice="required"` (#60882), DeepSeek V4/V3.2 (#58780), GLM-4.7 (#64535), Qwen3 (#64675). - Fixes: DeepSeek V4.1 (#62517, #64971, #62729, #62647), GLM-4.7 (#64615), Step3 (#65274), FunctionGemma (#63992), union/enum string parameters (#64518). - **Behavior** - Corrupt or oversized images and disabled local media return 400 instead of 500 (#63433, #60308, #64032). - Responses accepts incomplete assistant/reasoning history, e.g. from Codex (#35508). - Multi-template processors use the default template (#63606); an empty `tools` array is accepted like OpenAI (#65547). - The first streamed usage reports cached prompt tokens (#65036); plain completion stream frames render about 9× faster (#52875). - **Rust frontend** - Stateless Responses API (#63902) with namespace tools (#65853); `n > 1` (#65625); `--skip-tokenizer-init` (#64697). - Hybrid and external DP load balancing (#64451, #64450); native GLM-5.3 chat rendering (#62424). - Prompt block hashing off the engine's GIL (#63842); `--reasoning-effort-map` (#62312). - `--enable-log-outputs`, `--max-log-len`, `--root-path`, `--log-error-stack` (#63769, #64223, #64222, #65001). - More request, response and metric parity with Python (#65293, #65294, #65623, #65624, #64218, #64526, #63964, #65636).
Security, dependencies and build - **Security** - ReDoS in the validation-error sanitizer fixed (#52120). - FunAudioChat audio bounded to the profiled duration (#57411). - `/v1/systemone` honors `--trust-request-chat-template` (#64503). - Raised floors for filelock, OpenTelemetry, graphql-core and others (#63574). - **Dependencies** - PyTorch stays at 2.14.0. FlashInfer 0.7.3 (#65930). - `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0`, `tokenizers >= 0.23.3`, `timm >= 1.0.30` (#64779); `transformers >= 5.16.1, < 5.23.0` (#64049, #64529); `mistral-common >= 1.13.0` (#64169). - DeepEP 2.1 (#59844); DeepGEMM pin updates (#64411, #64580, #65494); FlashMLA and FlashKDA pins (#61971, #64759). - NIXL 1.5.2 (#64579, #64585); mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.14 (#65576); Run:ai Model Streamer 0.17.1 (#63174); `fastokens >= 0.3.5` for `VLLM_USE_FASTOKENS` (#65679). - ROCm: AITER v0.1.27 → v0.1.28.post1 (#63774, #65937). XPU: PyTorch 2.15 (#63977), triton-xpu 3.9.0 (#65047), vllm_xpu_kernels 0.1.17 (#60609). CPU: zentorch 2.14.0.2 (#65669). - **Build** - x86_64 CUDA wheel about 82 MB (about 25%) smaller, kernels unchanged (#65518). - Default CUDA image installs the AWS EFA userspace; the `-efa` image now only adds DeepEP for EFA (#65576); nightly EFA images as `vllm/vllm-openai:efa-nightly` (#64028). - One ROCm build and release pipeline, ROCm 10.0 only (#61939). - Source builds fetch `triton_kernels` from a tarball (#65162) and ship tuned kernel configs in the wheel (#64063). - CUDA `x.yf` arches no longer fall back to a lower minor (#66016).
All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults - **Model Runner V1 removed** (#63373). - `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` and `VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner` are gone; setting the env var to anything but `1` fails at startup. - Dropped with it: the V1 logits-processor API (`vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor` is the only interface), the `custom_class` speculative method, `use_heterogeneous_vocab`, `disable_padded_drafter_batch`, `parallel_drafting` outside DFlash/DSpark, PP with `external_launcher`, `NGramPerReqLogitsProcessor`, and x86 CPUs without Triton. - Deprecated: `parallel_drafting`, `capture_torch_profiler`, `enable_layerwise_nvtx_tracing`. - **Default `--block-size` is 64** instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit `--block-size` still wins. - **`gpu_memory_utilization` defaults to 1.0** when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704). - **ROCm 7.2** wheels and `-rocm72` images are no longer published (#61939). - **Removed:** - QuTLASS and the `fp_quant` method (#65230). - Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and `VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE`; use `--quantization humming` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` (#65542). - Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 (#64287); `disable_mtp_completeness_check` (#49459); the `refresh_derived_weights` hook (#65914). - **Dependencies:** `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` (#64779); `mistral-common >= 1.13.0` (#64169); XPU requires vllm_xpu_kernels 0.1.17 (#60609). - **Model and plugin code:** all `process_weights_after_loading` hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config `compute_hash()` replaced by `compile_factors()` / `hash_config()` (#65652). - **API behavior:** - llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569). - Canary transcription without `language` returns 400 (#65445). - An empty `tools` array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854). - `/v1/systemone` rejects request-supplied chat templates without `--trust-request-chat-template` (#64503). - LoRA adapters on modules vLLM does not wrap are refused (#63489); misconfigured NCCL weight transfer raises (#57022). - `vllm-rs serve` no longer reads `--data-parallel-rank` from `VLLM_DP_RANK` (#65369). - AITER fused shared experts with MiniMax M3 and DeepSeek V4 need `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1` (#61457). - **Still deprecated:** `--mamba-cache-mode` has no effect; its removal was postponed (#64838). - **New defaults:** - Extensible KV cache (#56492); block size 64 (#63231); best-effort NUMA binding (#61258). - Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill at 1024 or more prefill tokens (#63956); MLA decode up-projection before the A2A merge (#64994). - `VLLM_COMPILE_ON_ONE_RANK` (#63247); minimum valid EPLB `num_redundant_experts` (#30614). - HiSparse on the extensible KV cache (#65214); encoder CUDA graphs up to `encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget=5120`, eager above (#65227). - TRITON_ATTN on RDNA3/RDNA4 (#60418); MRV2 on non-Triton CPUs (#61995); `float32` Mamba SSM cache for Nemotron Omni (#63218); Zipf routing in `vllm bench forward` (#64167).
