We propose a two-timescale optimization framework, where the trajectory of the UAV is carried out on a large timescale, while the task reassignment and computing resource allocation are jointly optimized on a small timescale. The core objective is to maximize the long-term average system gain, which takes both energy consumption and task delay into account. To address the UAV trajectory optimization problem under large timescale constraints, we propose a constrained multi-agent deep reinforcement learning algorithm. For decision-making within small timescale, to jointly optimize task offloading decisions and computing resource allocation, we integrate convex optimization with a heuristic algorithm. Finally, we conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the proposed algorithms against the baseline, achieving a 24% reduction in latency and a 28% reduction in total system cost.
entries.title: Two-Timescale Trajectory Control, Task Reassignment and Resource Scheduling for Multi-UAV Cooperative Mobile Edge Computing

entries.abstract: We study Nash equilibrium learning in partially observable Markov games (POMGs), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which agents cannot fully observe the underlying state. Prior work in this setting relies on centralization or information sharing, and suffers from sample and computational complexity that scales exponentially in the number of players. We focus on a subclass of POMGs with independent state transitions, where agents remain coupled through their rewards, and assume that the underlying fully observed Markov game is a Markov potential game. For this class, we present an independent learning algorithm in which players, observing only their own actions and observations and without communication, jointly converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium. Due to partial observability, optimal policies may in general depend on the full action-observation history. Under a filter stability assumption, we show that policies based on finite history windows provide sufficient approximation guarantees. This enables us to approximate the POMG by a surrogate Markov game that is near-potential, leading to quasi-polynomial sample and computational complexity for independent Nash equilibrium learning in the underlying POMG.
entries.title: Independent Learning of Nash Equilibria in Partially Observable Markov Potential Games with Decoupled Dynamics

entries.abstract: Frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) is a laser pump-probe technique widely used to measure thermal properties at the micro- and nanoscale; however, it relies on a complex data analysis procedure that demands substantial domain expertise and is susceptible to subtle human errors. Here, we present Vibe-FDTR, an agent-oriented framework that enables large language model (LLM) agents to perform reliable and reproducible FDTR analyses directly from natural language requests. This framework couples a configuration-driven FDTR code package, which enforces physical and parametric consistency, with procedural agent skills that translate user intentions into organized and verifiable analysis steps. We evaluate Vibe-FDTR using a controlled benchmark with two levels: synthetic single-step tasks and real-data multi-step tasks based on measurements of gold-coated graphite samples. Across the two levels, agents using Vibe-FDTR achieve success rates of 100% and 98.9%, respectively. In sharp contrast, ablating skills (Code-agent) reduces performance to 91.4% and 36.7%, which drops further to 38.6% and 0% when the domain package is also omitted (Agent-only). Beyond success rate, Vibe-FDTR also reduces computational cost by 87.7% relative to the Code-agent variant and cuts execution time by more than 60%. Finally, an optional expert mode supports experimental planning via autonomous sensitivity and uncertainty evaluations, and formulates physically grounded recommendations for underspecified tasks. These results demonstrate that encapsulating domain code and expert knowledge into agent skills offers a promising route toward low-barrier, autonomous, and trustworthy thermal metrology.
entries.journal_ref: Advanced Scientific Instruments, 100049 (2026)
entries.title: Vibe-FDTR: An agent-oriented framework for reproducible frequency-domain thermoreflectance data analysis

entries.abstract: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.
entries.comment: 21 pages; updated author order and corresponding author contact information
entries.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces

entries.abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.
entries.journal_ref: NeurIPS 2026
entries.title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs

entries.abstract: Learning agents are becoming market participants, yet machine learning still treats the market as a fixed environment, although its payoff rule is the reward agents learn from. This position paper argues that financial AI should build HyperMarkets for human-AI collective intelligence, and not only the agents that trade in them: markets whose liquidity provision, information production, outcome determination, and trading rule are performed or adapted by learning agents and designed jointly toward explicit market-level objectives. In a pre-registered simulation with Claude agents trading for principals, joint design raises a market-level objective by 79% over separately tuned functions, through a trading rule that helps only when slow traders are present, and how evidence is paid for decides whether a stronger agent earns more for its principal. We state when fixed rules or non-market aggregation should be preferred and what findings would refute the case.
entries.title: The Market Is the Reward: Design Markets, Not Just Traders for Human-AI Collective Intelligence

entries.abstract: AI agents can generate as-built Building Information Models (BIMs) from reality-capture data, but the evidence required for accurate reconstruction remains unclear. This paper presents Agent2BIM, an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework, and evaluates seven capture configurations in a research laboratory and a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scene. Inputs include 360° panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared against TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity. In the laboratory, component recall ranged from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of components reconstructed from panoramas were within 20 cm of their reference positions, compared with 86% using smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recovered 11 - 43% of components, versus 75 - 93% for metric inputs. Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate inaccuracies. The results highlight the complementary roles of visual and metric evidence in agent-based Scan-to-BIM.
entries.title: Agent2BIM: A Systematic Evaluation of Reality-Capture Configurations and Prior Models for As-Built Modeling

entries.abstract: Simulations of LLM agent collectives usually summarise interaction as a pairwise contact network. We test that summary with a contact-matched intervention: the members, their initial stances and every pairwise contact count stay fixed while the meetings are reorganised, and each member gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present. Across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics, merging triads into five-person meetings (resize) moves group support more than reshuffling who meets in triads (regroup), although both move the same 60 dyadic exposures. The root-mean-square change is 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points (pp), larger for resize in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing also has a consistent direction: it amplifies the initial majority of the merged members by 1.72 pp, in every model, whereas regrouping has no direction (<= 0.03 pp). A contact network cannot represent regrouping at all, yet pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of its effect, and with identical weights they raise resize R^2 by 0.51-0.58 for two models. We show that the gap between the two placements is an exact Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout, bounded by how much a member's predicted logits vary across meetings; this dispersion tracks the gap with log-log r=0.97 and tells a modeller when contact counts are a safe summary. Meeting format is a first-class variable for LLM social simulation.
entries.title: Same Contacts, Different Rooms:Meeting Format Shapes LLM Group Influence Beyond Pairwise Contact Counts

entries.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.
entries.title: SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum

entries.abstract: Task success can hide process anomalies in real-world agent executions. An agent may pass the final task oracle while still accumulating unresolved ambiguity, unsafe external writes, ignored errors, weakly grounded commitments, or capability-boundary overcommitment. We study this mismatch as the Outcome-Process Gap and introduce OpenClawBench, a large-scale dataset for measuring and supervising process-side anomalies in real agent execution processes. OpenClawBench is built from BFCL-driven OpenClaw sessions produced by 6 source models and contains 31,264 annotated trajectories. FullTax converts the aligned trajectories into structured anomaly supervision: binary labels, supporting evidence, onset/span localization, severity, recoverability, and a 5-class anomaly taxonomy. Using OpenClawBench, we make the Outcome-Process Gap measurable. Among 31,135 oracle-passing executions, 2,904 (9.33%) are still labeled process-anomalous under FullTax. Within oracle-passing executions that contain high-risk process evidence, 1,765 of 1,904 (92.70%) are labeled anomalous. On Gold-300, a test subset labeled independently by two human annotators, silver labels match the final human binary label on 93.3% of trajectories. A LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 3 12B detector trained on the high-confidence FullTax supervised pool reaches binary F1=0.729 on the cleaner-labels silver test split (n=2,646). It outperforms the GPT-5.4 frontier reference by +0.302 absolute, the no-fine-tuning base by +0.357, and wins on all six source-model agent slices. The gain comes from calibration rather than higher recall: zero-shot detectors over-flag at 42-50% against a 14.8% label rate, while the fine-tuned detector predicts anomalies 18.2% of the time. Together, OpenClawBench turns real agent execution logs into auditable and reusable supervision for studying, diagnosing, and operationally monitoring runtime agent reliability.
entries.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track. 42 pages, 1 figure. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/YangzeLiu/OpenClawBench Code: https://github.com/YangzeLiu/OpenClawBench
entries.title: OpenClawBench: Benchmarking Process-side Anomalies in Real-world Agent Execution Trajectories

entries.abstract: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.
entries.title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL

entries.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for first-principles materials simulation. We report empirical findings from DFT-Agent Bench, a benchmark of 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks spanning relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor pipelines over multiple material tiers. Each task carries a QE-derived ground truth with public-reference cross-checks where available, and a provenance audit checks whether the required QE execution contract was met. Under one execution harness, we compare a near-bare ReAct baseline with a bundled v5.1 scaffold on two models. The complete scaffold improves bands+DOS by +0.08/+0.11 and d-electron vc-relax by +0.17 on both models, while high-scoring relaxation and equation-of-state cells leave little room for improvement. The elastic result is model-dependent (0.18 to 0.40 for deepseek-v4-pro and 0.62 to 0.59 for claude-opus-4-8). A fixed 100-task analysis with retrieval disabled supports the aggregate pattern: the fully frozen DeepSeek comparison gains +0.17, while the Opus comparison gains +0.10 against a historical pool baseline (p < 0.001). The provenance gate catches incomplete or unmarked executions that can receive high rubric scores; it is an execution-contract check, not a test for intentional fraud. These results characterize the evaluated DFT workflows. The anonymous review artifact contains the frozen diagnostic slice, prompts, scorer, and solver revisions: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/231e31re91287h/README.md.
entries.title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT

entries.abstract: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.
entries.title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition

entries.abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
entries.comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; archive: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23636508
entries.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors

entries.abstract: We study first-order learning dynamics in Bayesian signaling games, a minimal extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information. In these games, a Sender observes a private type and chooses a signal, after which a Receiver forms a posterior belief and selects an action. This Bayesian belief update makes the induced learning field fundamentally different from the affine game-gradient fields of normal-form games. Empirically, we find a sharp dichotomy: standard online learning algorithms reliably converge to strict Perfect Bayesian Equilibria (PE), but not to non-strict ones. We show that this behavior cannot be explained by the global geometric conditions commonly used to prove last-iterate convergence, such as monotonicity or the Minty variational inequality. Indeed, these conditions can fail even in binary signaling games. Instead, we identify the relevant local geometry. Our main result characterizes variational stability in finite signaling games: a PE is variationally stable if and only if it is strict. This yields local last-iterate convergence guarantees for online mirror descent and regularized dual averaging near every strict PE. We then study global average-iterate convergence and identify a class of signaling games in which coarse-trigger regret-minimizing dynamics converge to the unique PE. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments comparing projected gradient ascent, mirror-based methods, optimistic variants, and PPO across canonical signaling-game families. The results position signaling games as a compact testbed for understanding how Bayesian belief formation reshapes the convergence geometry of multi-agent learning.
entries.title: On the Convergence of First-Order Methods in Signaling Games

entries.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spectral response that shifts during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.
entries.comment: 27 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables; v2 adds fine-grid Stage IV trailing-plasma timing and timestep-contraction controls, load-versus-background energy accounting, and expanded numerical audits; code at https://github.com/tomzhu0225/simjecture
entries.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch

entries.abstract: Tool-connected agents need execution-time invariants that hold even when a model follows an adversarial instruction. We formulate eight execution-layer invariants (I1-I8) covering structured authority, canonical resource resolution, principal and delegation binding, handle lifecycle, explicit source-to-target transfer, request-correlated denial evidence, and single-use approval state. To test whether these protections require a centralized runtime or follow from the invariants themselves, we compare HCP, an in-memory runtime with managed handles and tasks, against an independent gateway/server ACL (B3) enforcing the same I1-I8 contract over identical grants and labels. Both block 18 modeled violations and complete 25 workflows, while 16 source-code ablations pinpoint the checks responsible. Outside our scripted corpus, we test three boundaries. First, on 24 held-out AgentDojo tasks with live models, DeepSeek reaches attacker goals in 4 direct sessions while both controllers deny every attacker call; however, strict reference-derived grants also deny 40 non-attacker calls, and first-divergence replay under an approve-all control reaches 4 new attacker goals. Second, across 132 conditions on unmodified ChainCaps and Playwright MCP servers, per-call grants block ungranted writes but cannot stop a secret passed as an ordinary argument to an authorized sink; session source budgets block that copy but refuse unrelated actions; and explicit handle pipes or sealed reads block handle-mediated exfiltration while preserving unrelated workflows. Third, on a matched MCP backend, HCP adds 0.13 ms per workflow outside MCP calls while retaining 7.7 MB of state over one thousand workflows versus 0.7 MB for B3. Identical decisions across HCP and B3 show that enforcing explicit I1-I8 invariants at controlled entrances secures tool execution across centralized and gateway designs.
entries.comment: v2: Expanded evaluation with an independent gateway baseline, live-model AgentDojo experiments, and tests on third-party MCP servers. Includes supplementary appendices and machine-readable results
entries.title: From Tool Connection to Execution Control: Benchmarking Security Invariants in MCP-Style Agent Runtimes

entries.abstract: As enterprise systems grow in scale and complexity, manual log analysis and conventional SIEM tools struggle to keep pace with the volume and diversity of incidents. To address this challenge, this paper proposed a multi-agent AI framework supporting in analyzing the system log to trace the attack forensic in the system more effectively and efficiently. The framework is designed using n8n platform and Gemini large language model. The framework consists of 7 AI agent layers. Each agent work on a specific task. When the task is done, the agent will forward the result to the output-associated agent of the next layer. The multi agent model improves the analysis velocity, so it is able to support numerous log analysis requirement at the same time. We deployed 16 test cases to test operation of the multi agent workflow, and evaluate the accuracy per test case and the operative performance. The result findings are very promising.
entries.comment: 14th International Conference on Multidisciplinary Research (ICMR 2026), ISBN 978-974-474-120-2, Thaksin University Publisher, Bangkok, Thailand, pp. 63-80, 2026 (Published)
entries.title: An Agentic Multi-Agent Framework for System Log Anomaly Detection

entries.abstract: This case study presents IF: CARGO, an experimental puzzle game that uses a large language model as a semantic compiler rather than an autonomous game-playing agent. Players author IF/THEN rules in natural language, which the model translates into a constrained command schema for deterministic validation and execution by the game engine. This architecture creates a playable loop of expression, execution, observation, and revision, framing AI interaction as semantic debugging. A mixed-methods playtest with 24 participants across eight levels examined player attempts, thinking time, perceived controllability, adjustability, and interpretations of the AI's role. Results suggest that players generally understood the model as a translation intermediary and could revise their strategies through feedback, while periodic commands, multi-robot coordination, and rule-priority mechanics created greater cognitive and diagnostic demands. The study proposes a practical pattern for AI-native gameplay: constrain natural-language input, preserve player authorship, and ensure deterministic execution.
entries.comment: Accepted to 2026 AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment (AIIDE)
entries.title: IF:CARGO: LLM-Based Semantic Compilation for Al-Native Rule Programming Games

entries.abstract: Disordered hyperuniform systems are characterized by an anomalously strong suppression of long-wavelength density fluctuations. As a result, these unusual materials behave as though virtually incompressible, even though the particle arrangement itself can remain fully disordered at short range. This peculiar state of matter has been the topic of intense research in physics and mathematics in recent years. Another flourishing research arena is active matter, composed of self-propelled agents that convert energy into motion. While the two fields remained largely disjunct for a long time, the paper by Lei and coworkers (2019) created a link between hyperuniformity and active matter by demonstrating that interacting circle swimmers self-organize into disordered hyperuniform structures. Inspired by this work, many other examples of hyperuniformity in active matter have been identified. We shall describe the impact and outgrowth of this development, and give a brief perspective on further links between hyperuniformity and active matter.
entries.journal_ref: KIM REVIEW 4, 5 (2026)
entries.title: Hyperuniformity in active matter

entries.abstract: When agents organize records into folders, they may correctly group the excerpts of a design proposal yet place the proposal under the wrong owning group. Existing agent benchmarks do not directly measure such higher-level errors. We introduce InfoOrgBench, a benchmark of 150 tasks in which agents organize scattered records from meeting recaps, issue threads and design proposals into hierarchies. Integrity checks verify that every record is preserved, and a Structure Score measures agreement with the source hierarchy at every level, independent of folder names and order. We evaluate 45 systems that pair nine models with five agent harnesses. The best system scores 83.2 out of 100, but no system exceeds 78 on meeting recaps or issue threads. Model choice affects scores far more than harness choice: model means span about 27 points, whereas the average effect of each harness is below one point. More importantly, parent-level relations have higher error rates than leaf-level relations in all three domains. In design proposals, nearly half of the outputs analyzed by level make exactly this kind of error. These results show that evaluating information organization requires measuring higher-level relations separately from record preservation and local grouping.
entries.title: InfoOrgBench: Can Agents Turn Scattered Information into Coherent Hierarchies?

entries.abstract: We present RoboLineage, an agent-native data lifecycle governance system for robot policy iteration. Modern robot policies improve through repeated data collection, review, retraining, evaluation, and release decisions, but the evidence connecting these steps is often scattered across local tools, scripts, and expert memory. RoboLineage makes this lifecycle explicit by representing rollouts, reviews, dataset decisions, training runs, policy metadata, evaluations, deployment recommendations, and next-collection plans as typed lineage artifacts. Agents interpret embodied rollout evidence, adapt accepted data to existing training stacks, maintain data health, and summarize cross-iteration state under explicit artifact boundaries. In real-robot manipulation workflows, RoboLineage makes routine policy iteration faster and more auditable while maintaining downstream policy performance. We open source RoboLineage as a lightweight lifecycle layer for different robot embodiments and training families. Project page: https://robolineage.github.io/
entries.title: RoboLineage: Agent-Native Data Lifecycle Governance Across Robot Policy Iterations

entries.abstract: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.
entries.comment: Accepted manuscript. 18 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables. Code and dataset: https://github.com/TUMAMX/agriquery/tree/main/ManualSync
entries.journal_ref: Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, 112595 (2026)
entries.title: Machine-Readable Operator Manuals over the ISO 11783 Network for Offline, Multilingual LLM Assistance

entries.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents produce long, multi-turn trajectories, making gradient-based post-training memory-intensive. Evolution strategies (ES) enable memory-efficient full-parameter post-training without backpropagation and can eventually match the performance of gradient-based reinforcement learning (RL). However, resource-constrained settings typically offer only a few GPUs, so the high GPU-hour requirements of ES translate into prohibitively long training times. To address this, we introduce Cooperative Parameter-subspace Evolution Strategy (CoPES), a cooperative coevolutionary method that decomposes the full parameter space into lower-dimensional subspaces and searches over them cooperatively to improve optimization efficiency. On Qwen3.5-4B math, CoPES recovers 92% of full-parameter GRPO's validation-accuracy gain within the GPU-hour budget of GRPO's best validation checkpoint, versus 67% for standard ES. Its theoretical GPU memory requirement is less than one-eighth that of full-parameter GRPO. It consistently outperforms standard ES and LoRA-based GRPO on all evaluated pass@k metrics across five math benchmarks. CoPES's gains extend to Qwen3.5-9B with unchanged optimization hyperparameters and to multi-hop QA. These results demonstrate an improved trade-off between memory requirements and training time for agentic LLM post-training under resource constraints. The code is open-sourced in https://github.com/MetaronWang/CoPES
entries.title: Cooperative Coevolution for Resource-Constrained Agentic LLM Post-Training

entries.abstract: Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.
entries.title: M3FT: Micro-Macro-Micro Reasoning for Multi-Agent Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures Trading

entries.abstract: Agents that learn from experience improve at optimization modeling by storing solved trajectories and reusing them as skills. A wrong trajectory that enters the library can be retrieved for many later problems, and a stream of new problems carries no ground-truth answers that could keep it out. Existing learners admit trajectories by matching known optima, and label-free substitutes such as execution success or agreement at one instance admit wrong models. We introduce AdmitOR, a label-free admission gate. It generates models from three model families and solves each on the stated problem and on instances with resampled parameters. It keeps the largest group of models whose optimal values agree on every instance and that spans more than one family. A threshold fitted on solver-verified problems maps this agreement to acceptance, abstention, or escalation, with a finite-sample bound on the false-discovery rate of accepted values. Inside a recent skill learner, AdmitOR raises admission precision from 0.871 under majority vote to 0.927. Its library is the smallest of the four compared and has the highest macro accuracy on five benchmarks. An ablation traces the gain to an accepted value external to the learner. One program from the learner's own model already raises precision to 0.923, and agreement across families raises it further. With one candidate per family, resampling can withhold a certificate but cannot change its value, and the values it withholds are wrong far more often than those it keeps, on the stream and on the solver-verified calibration set. The false-discovery bound holds on the calibration set but not on the benchmark stream. An audit traces every false certificate to a benchmark text that omits or rounds the numbers needed to reproduce the labeled answer, or to a label error. A label-free check of the extracted numbers against the text flags most omitted-number cases.
entries.comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/junbolian/AdmitOR
entries.title: Admission Without Answers: Label-Free Certification and Experience Learning for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling

entries.abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.
entries.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control

entries.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can recognize events in images and parse sentences, but it remains unclear when they bind visual Agent-Patient structure to linguistic semantic roles across languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction. We introduce ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic that pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders. The evaluation separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions. Across eight recent open-weight VLMs, ROLECUE reveals a structured spectrum: some models fail visual or linguistic component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent and several show component-joint gaps in which reliable image-only and text-only role predictions do not survive direct joint inference. The largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, with final bootstrap intervals confirming that the effect is not a point-estimate artifact. These results reveal multilingual component-joint performance gaps and acceptance biases hidden by aggregate VLM benchmarks and show why component diagnostics are necessary before interpreting joint multimodal errors.
entries.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027, Evaluations and Datasets Track
entries.title: ROLECUE: Diagnosing Cross-Lingual Role-Binding Failures in Vision-Language Models

entries.abstract: Radio resource management in dense networks is subject to budgets that must hold on every realized trajectory, carried by different agent groups: an energy budget at each base station (BS) and a handover budget at each user, coupled through the association decisions that consume both. Constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) handles such budgets using Lagrangian multipliers updated across episodes or Lyapunov virtual queues updated per slot, but their relative behavior under coupled two-sided constraints remains unclear. We formulate this problem and introduce a windowed proportional-fairness objective that captures the temporal distribution of service beyond the classical horizon-average formulation. We characterize the distinct budget-regulation timescales of the two mechanisms through complementary theoretical bounds and identify queue-price buildup as a key mechanism governing finite-horizon budget pacing. Using a common heterogeneous MARL architecture, we compare three utility surrogates and both constraint-handling mechanisms. The results show that utility design primarily determines throughput and fairness, whereas constraint-price dynamics govern training efficiency and budget pacing. Under the default setting, the queue-based PF policy reaches near-final performance after a single training episode, but its unscaled penalty can lead to delayed pacing under tight budgets. Guided by the analysis, we show that queue-price calibration reduces the empirical drift constant by an order of magnitude and substantially narrows the performance gap to Lagrangian methods, which adapt constraint prices across episodes at higher training cost. These findings provide practical design guidelines for constrained MARL.
entries.comment: Revised version with updated title, theoretical analysis, and experiments. 14 pages
entries.title: Lagrangian or Lyapunov? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Coupled Finite-Horizon Constraints

entries.abstract: Deploying language models as autonomous agents requires more than per-task accuracy: when an agent faces a queue of problems under a finite token budget, it must decide which to attempt, in what order, and how much compute to commit to each, all before any execution feedback is available. This is the prospective form of metacognitive control studied for decades in human cognition, yet whether language models possess it remains largely untested. We introduce TRIAGE, an evaluation framework in which a model receives a task pool and a token budget calibrated to its own baseline cost, and commits to a single ordered plan that jointly encodes selection, sequencing, and per-problem allocation. Plans are scored against an oracle built from the measured solvability and token costs of the model, using triage efficiency normalized between random and oracle performance, together with normalized regret relative to the oracle. We evaluate frontier and open-source models, with and without reasoning enabled, across competition mathematics, graduate-level science, code generation, and expert multidisciplinary knowledge, and find that current language models exhibit substantial gaps in prospective metacognitive control, revealing a previously unmeasured capability dimension with direct implications for resource-efficient agent deployment.
entries.title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs under Resource Constraints

entries.abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.
entries.comment: 23 pages total: 8-page main paper plus 15-page supplementary material; 1 main-paper figure and 3 main-paper tables. Equal contribution. Code available at: https://github.com/SummerRainET2008/DRCB
entries.title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes

entries.abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
entries.title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable

entries.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.
entries.title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach for improving reasoning in language and vision-language models, yet its strongest successes still depend heavily on ground-truth supervision (e.g., verifiable reward). Such annotations are costly to obtain and become increasingly scarce as reasoning capabilities advance beyond what humans can reliably evaluate. Self-rewarding RL reduces this dependence by enabling models to derive reward signals from their own completions. However, training solely on self-generated feedback can reinforce existing biases, reduce response diversity, and ultimately lead to homogenized responses and training collapse. In this work, we show that unsupervised reasoning can emerge through cooperative multi-agent training. We introduce Co-RL, a framework in which multiple decoupled models, sharing no parameters, are simultaneously optimized through RL using rewards derived from the other agent. We further show that increasing cohort diversity, through heterogeneous model families, sizes, and rephrased training samples, reduces the correlated errors that drive self-reinforcing feedback loops. This diversity consistently improves reasoning performance and mitigates training collapse. Without any ground-truth labels, Co-RL improves the base models by 3.0-7.9% on average across seven benchmarks and by 1.6-4.4% across four multimodal benchmarks. It also outperforms the prior state-of-the-art multi-agent RL method CoMAS by 4.0% and the self-rewarding vision-language RL method MM-UPT by 2.0%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Diverse-CoRL/Co-RL and website at https://williamium3000.github.io/Co-RL.
entries.comment: 31 pages. Code: https://github.com/Diverse-CoRL/Co-RL. Project page: https://williamium3000.github.io/Co-RL/
entries.title: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. Existing skill backdoor attacks typically assume direct manipulation of the victim's skills, which is impractical when skills are constructed internally by a trusted evolver. In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks, inducing the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. Since the attacker controls neither skill induction nor downstream execution, a natural approach is to iteratively optimize poisoned tasks based on attack success. However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Our code is available at https://github.com/ventr1c/BadEvolve.
entries.title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
entries.title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks

entries.abstract: VLM-based agents solve complex tasks by iteratively interacting with environments, and their effectiveness depends heavily on how the environment exposes information and provides tools for acting on it. However, constructing an effective environment for complex multimodal document question answering remains challenging: documents usually span many pages, with multimodal contents distributed across hierarchical sections and linked by cross-modal associations, while existing methods organize documents into structured representations that address only the information side of the environment and lack tools aligned with the structure, limiting agents' ability to fully exploit it. We observe that file systems naturally combine structure organization with aligned tools: directories and files encode document structure, while file operations provide rich tools to access file contents. Building on this insight, we propose DocFS, a file-system-based agentic framework that reorganizes raw documents as file systems, where directories mirror the section hierarchy and explicit links connect text with figures, tables, and equations. Based on well-established file system tools such as navigation, search, and reading, agents can iteratively explore the document structure, locate relevant evidence, and understand fine-grained local information. Paired with Qwen3.5-Plus, DocFS achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMLongBench-Doc and FinRAGBench-V, outperforming the strongest baselines by 2.9 and 4.3 percentage points, respectively, and is up to 10.3x faster with up to 10.1x fewer tokens than the strongest baseline during reasoning.
entries.title: DocFS: File Systems as Agentic Reasoning Environments for Complex Multimodal Document Question Answering

entries.abstract: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand---in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5\%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5\% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3$\times$. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.
entries.title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models

entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language processing but struggle to interact with external environments. Tool learning provides a promising way to extend LLMs into actionable agents, where tool selection is a critical prerequisite for successful tool use. Existing work often assumes a small or predefined set of tools, leaving large-scale tool selection underexplored. Real-world repositories contain a vast and diverse array of tools, making it difficult for LLMs to effectively search, distinguish, and compose tools under context-length constraints. We identify large-scale tool selection as a new challenge for agentic reinforcement learning, highlighting that existing RL methods for knowledge-based question answering are inadequate for selecting tools while considering compatibility. To address this challenge, we propose ToolSearcher, a novel RL framework for effective multi-turn search and fine-grained optimization in large-scale tool selection. Specifically, we introduce category-constrained tool discrimination to improve the model's ability to distinguish functionally similar tools, event-level search modeling to explicitly optimize the discovery of target tools during multi-turn search, and trajectory-aligned credit allocation to provide fine-grained reward signals for different stages of the search-selection process. Extensive experiments on large-scale tool selection benchmarks demonstrate that ToolSearcher consistently outperforms a set of strong baselines in challenging settings involving iterative search and complex tool composition.
entries.title: ToolSearcher: Optimizing Tool Selection at Scale via Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: Clinical decision-making is inherently experience-driven: physicians progressively refine their reasoning by synthesizing patient history, multimodal observations, and prior diagnostic experiences across interactions. In contrast, current multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based medical AI agents largely operate as stateless inference systems, generating decisions independently for each interaction without retaining or internalizing experiential knowledge. This discrepancy limits their ability to progressively improve reasoning reliability through usage and adapt to longitudinal patient contexts in real-world clinical workflows. In this study, we propose Medical Structured Multimodal Memory (MSM-Mem), an agentic memory framework that enables medical AI agents to evolve through accumulated clinical experiences. MSM-Mem organizes heterogeneous clinical experiences into semantic, episodic, and visual memory and incrementally updates them during inference, allowing the agent to retrieve prior experiences to inform current reasoning and progressively refine decision-making over time. Evaluations on MoE-LLaVA backbones demonstrate consistent performance improve- ments with further gains observed through continued usage. In general, MSM-Mem offers a viable pathway toward medical AI agents capable of evolving their reasoning competence in a manner analogous to the way clinicians learn from practice over time.
entries.journal_ref: GenAI4Health @ NeurIPS 2026
entries.title: MSM-Mem: A Universal Medical Structured Multimodal Memory Framework for Medical AI Agents

entries.abstract: Studies of how long lines of code live, including lines written by AI agents, rest on choices that look technical: when a line counts as gone, what to do with lines still alive, whether to pool projects, and how to evaluate a model. We studied 32.5 million line births in 120 TypeScript repositories and got several of these choices wrong at first. For ten of them, we compare the result as we first computed it, or as commonly done, with the result after correction. All ten change conclusions, or would have. Six were our own mistakes. Counting moved and rewritten lines as dead shortens a line's median life from 3.0 years to 1.3. Counting any change as a death hides an outcome that can be predicted: within-project concordance falls from 0.71 to 0.56. Regressing observed lifetimes discards three quarters of the lines. Keeping rewritten lines at risk makes protective effects grow with age. Lines are born and removed together, so treating them as independent misleads twice: nine of fifteen effects look significant only under that assumption, and a split by file makes a barely predictable outcome look good (within-project concordance 0.71 instead of 0.61). After the corrections, removal depends on a line's age and project, but our models could barely rank it within a project. Local revision they could rank (0.71). Obvious cases aside, the top 1% of a project's new lines are revised at 2.3 times the base rate. Each pitfall leaves a symptom; we give a checklist.
entries.comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Corrects results of arXiv:2606.04993
entries.title: Mismeasuring the Life of a Line of Code: Lessons Learned the Hard Way

entries.abstract: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on DDBench's hardest case-set. Second, bounded debugging context lifts aggregate pass rate by +19.0 pp, and the lift is asymmetric: weaker models gain more in pass rate, while stronger models gain more in efficiency. Third, debugging context requires careful curation, as even faithful debugging context can anchor a strong model on the wrong layer of the system when its observation sits far from the fault.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages for the main body (7 figures, 3 tables), 23 pages for the appendix
entries.title: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems

entries.abstract: Large skill libraries are now standard equipment for LLM agents, and which subset reaches the prompt decides what the agent can do. Enumeration and top-$K$ embedding retrieval both treat skills as independent documents, assuming relevance is a property of one skill at a time. It is not: skills depend on, conflict with, specialize, and duplicate one another, so the closest match to a task can name it while omitting a prerequisite it needs. Graph retrieval encodes these relations but spends them in a fixed pipeline, handing the agent an opaque bundle. We present SkillDAG, which exposes a typed skill graph to the LLM as an agent-callable interface rather than consuming it for the agent: search returns vector matches, typed-edge neighbors, and conflict signals, and a propose-then-commit protocol lets it register execution-backed edges as it works. Across two benchmarks and three model families, SkillDAG outperforms full-library prompting, vector retrieval, and Graph-of-Skills, gaining +14.3 points of ALFWorld success and tying only at ceiling; its ranking holds flat across a $10\times$ pool expansion that degrades the fixed pipeline. Inter-skill structure, these results suggest, is worth more to an agent that can query and revise it than to a retriever that consumes it.
entries.comment: In *The 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP, Findings)*, 2026
entries.title: SkillDAG: Self-Evolving Typed Skill Graphs for LLM Skill Selection at Scale

entries.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present SecureGARD, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. SecureGARD grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. SecureGARD evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action-state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate SecureGARD on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. SecureGARD achieves a 0% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.
entries.title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

entries.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.
entries.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents

entries.abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.
entries.comment: Submitted to intelligent computing for embodied AI and robotics
entries.title: ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation

entries.abstract: Predicting where multiple agents will move next is fundamental to autonomous driving, robotics, and any system that must share space with people safely. Modern stochastic predictors read off inter-agent interactions once from the observed past and keep that view fixed throughout the generative rollout, so the reciprocal geometric constraints that emerge as the joint future sharpens are not re-examined. We address this gap with SRA (Spatial Reasoning Adapter), a modular graph denoiser that is integrated into existing diffusion and flow-matching predictors without redesigning their generative cores. At every reverse step, SRA reads the host's current future estimate, builds a sparse Euclidean interaction graph on the predicted trajectories, and returns a residual correction to the host's decoding path. Our adapter consists of three core components: a sparse neighborhood retrieved with a learned query-key score and a geometric bias, a future-conditioned relational feature recomputed on the evolving prediction, and uncertainty-weighted message passing where confident agents act as anchors for uncertain ones. We instantiate SRA on three structurally different hosts (LED, MID, and MoFlow) across four multi-agent benchmarks: SDD, NBA, Soccer, and Football. SRA improves ADE for every host on every dataset, with average gains of 5.8% in ADE and 7.0% in FDE. A cumulative ablation shows that the three components act as one mechanism: only together do they improve every host on every sports dataset, indicating that spatial reasoning over the model's own evolving future, weighted by how far that future can be trusted, is broadly useful across denoising architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/Jaewoo97/SRA.
entries.title: SRA: Spatial Reasoning Adapter via Evolving Social Interaction Graphs for Trajectory Prediction

entries.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.
entries.comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Position Paper Track
entries.title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate

entries.abstract: Tool-use language agents are evaluated on benchmarks that assume clean inputs, unambiguous tool registries, and reliable APIs. Real deployments violate all these assumptions: user typos propagate into hallucinated tool names, a misconfigured request timeout can stall an agent indefinitely, and duplicate tool names across servers can freeze an SDK. We study these failures as a sim-to-real gap in the tool-use partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where deployment noise enters through the observation, action space, reward-relevant metadata, or transition dynamics. We introduce AgentRobustBench, a benchmark with 22 perturbation types organized by these four POMDP components, each grounded in a verified GitHub issue or documented tool-calling failure. Across 21 models from 1.5B to 32B parameters (including the closed-source o4-mini), the robustness profile is sharply uneven: observation perturbations reduce accuracy by less than 5%, while reward-relevant and transition perturbations reduce accuracy by roughly 40% and 30%, respectively; scale alone does not close these gaps. We then propose ToolRL-DR, a domain-randomization reinforcement learning (RL) recipe that trains a tool-use agent on perturbation-augmented trajectories spanning the three statically encodable POMDP components. On a 3B backbone, ToolRL-DR-Full retains roughly three-quarters of clean accuracy and reaches an aggregate perturbed accuracy comparable to open-source 14B function-calling baselines while substantially narrowing the gap to o4-mini. It closes approximately 27% of the Transition gap despite never seeing transition perturbations in training, suggesting that RL on adversarial static tool-use inputs induces a more persistent retry policy that transfers to unseen runtime failures. Code, dataset, checkpoints, and leaderboard are accessible through our GitHub repository.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Camera-ready version with updated content, acknowledgments, and resource links. Benchmark renamed to AgentRobustBench. Code, dataset, checkpoints, and leaderboard: https://github.com/WillChow66/AgentRobustBench
entries.title: AgentRobustBench: A Sim-to-Real Benchmark and Domain-Randomized RL Recipe for Tool-Use Agents

entries.abstract: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints.
