PyCapsule features sophisticated prompt inference, iterative error handling, and case testing, ensuring high generation stability, safety, and correctness. Empirically, PyCapsule achieves up to 5.7% improvement in success rate on HumanEval, 14.6% on HumanEval-ET, and up to 24.5% on BigCodeBench compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, PyCapsule enables the open-source Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B model to surpass the standalone performance of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 on HumanEval and MBPP while requiring an average of fewer than 2 API calls per problem compared to up to 17 in competing frameworks. PyCapsule demonstrates broader impacts on advancing lightweight and efficient code generation, making competitive automated programming attainable with cost-effective, locally deployable open-source models.
entries.title: Large Language Model Guided Self-Debugging Code Generation

entries.abstract: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of schema.json + notes.md, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.
entries.title: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis

entries.abstract: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.
entries.title: Who Schedules Agent Memory? A Sidecar Approach to Long-Horizon Tasks

entries.abstract: Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.
entries.title: Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents

entries.abstract: Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.
entries.title: Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents

entries.abstract: Radio maps provide spatial knowledge of wireless environments to assess coverage, manage spectrum use, and support connectivity-aware mobility. Recent advances in embodied intelligence (EI) offer a promising approach to radio map reconstruction by enabling agents to perceive the environment and autonomously adjust their survey paths toward safe, reachable locations. However, a single agent remains constrained by limited endurance and onboard computing capacity, limiting measurement collection and reconstruction performance. Swarm cooperation can support more efficient radio mapping over larger areas by sharing observations and coordinating members' sampling. This article first explores the capabilities and applications of cooperative embodied agents. A cooperative radio map reconstruction framework is then presented, together with its key enabling techniques. Case study results illustrate how scene perception supports access to informative sampling locations and how air--ground cooperation improves reconstruction through complementary measurements and mobile support. The article concludes with open challenges and future research directions for reliable and efficient embodied cooperative radio mapping in complex environments.
entries.title: Embodied AI for Radio Mapping: From Solo to Swarm

entries.abstract: Structural phase transitions underpin ferroelectric and multiferroic functionality, but constructing interpretable energy landscapes remains dependent on specialist expertise. Predicting this behaviour rests on Landau free energies expanded in symmetry-adapted order parameters: their coefficients classify a transition, expose the couplings between distortions, set switching paths and barriers, and parametrize phase-field and effective-Hamiltonian models at larger scales. Obtaining these coefficients from first principles means sampling the Born--Oppenheimer energy surface along symmetry-derived structural paths, which requires crystallographic analysis, reliable structure generation and extensive computation, especially for coupled multidimensional order parameters. Here we introduce IRIS, an agentic workflow that converts plain-language requests and crystal structures into symmetry-adapted energy landscapes and fitted Landau energy models. Deterministic gates govern acceptance of structures, calculations and fits, while language models interpret requests and select constrained recovery actions. Applications across six compounds include a six-dimensional BiFeO$_3$ landscape that separates competition between polar and tilt amplitudes from directional locking and ranks homogeneous switching pathways. Controlled replays detected all 53 injected faults; disabling gates allowed 14 silent errors. Four prospective BaTiO$_3$ runs produced fitted landscapes from 96 density-functional calculations in 34 minutes total without intervening human decisions. IRIS makes physical model construction a reusable computational capability and provides a framework for scientific automation grounded in explicit verification.
entries.title: IRIS: an agentic eye on symmetry-derived paths and energy landscapes of structural phase transitions

entries.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
entries.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models

entries.abstract: Complex systems are increasingly explored through simulation-driven workflows that combine physics-based and empirical models with optimization and analytics. Despite their power, these workflows face two central obstacles: high computational cost from repeated expensive simulator runs, and limited transparency when decisions rely on opaque black-box models. We propose a workflow that addresses both challenges by training lightweight emulators on compact designs of experiments that (i) provide fast, low-latency approximations of expensive simulators, (ii) enable rigorous uncertainty quantification, and (iii) support global and local eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) analyses. This work formalizes a methodological bridge accommodating continuous, categorical, and integer variables across diverse domains, from engineering design to socio-environmental agent-based models. To validate surrogate explanations and examine how faithfully they reflect simulator behavior, we introduce a comparative methodology incorporating active validation filters, including explanation consistency and aleatoric uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, we provide practical guidelines for coupling experimental designs with emulator training to select architectures that balance computational efficiency with interpretability. We demonstrate the framework across two contrasting paradigms: a deterministic multidisciplinary design simulation of a hybrid-electric aircraft and a stochastic agent-based simulation of urban segregation. Results show that coupling surrogates with XAI enables large-scale exploration in seconds, reveals critical nonlinear interactions, and highlights potential design and policy levers while establishing consistent explanations across architectures.
entries.comment: version 2, after first reviews, second round. Thx to J. Levy for help
entries.title: Surrogate Modeling and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Complex Systems: A Workflow for Automated Simulation Exploration

entries.abstract: ZenBrain is a seven-layer, neuroscience-derived architecture for agent memory in LLM agents. An open library holds the seven layers, a MemoryCoordinator and nine foundational algorithms; six Predictive Memory Architecture components run in a private production system. In the open library at version 0.5.1, decay acts only on working memory and nothing is replayed. Ablating one component at a time exposes an effect we call cooperative masking. The ablation runs in a simulation harness that switches fifteen components as stand-ins at simulated values, not as production code. Under moderate load, fourteen of the fifteen ablations look costless. Raising decay, the horizon, the corpus and the queries, with no change to the components, moves ten of the fifteen in the same direction on all ten seeds - nine losses (Delta-Q down to -93.7%) and one gain. With ten seeds this is the one p-value the normal approximation of the Wilcoxon test can reach (5.06e-3), and it does not pass the Bonferroni-corrected level for fifteen contrasts (3.33e-3). On LongMemEval_S (500 questions), the evaluated ZenBrain arm - a Python port of a scoring class from our test harness, not the seven-layer system - answers 47.7% of the questions correctly under a binary judge (95% interval [43.3, 52.1]). With the compared systems' adapters repaired, Letta reaches 48.4% and Mem0 47.2%. ZenBrain reaches 91.3% of a full-context baseline's accuracy with 1/109.7 of its input tokens in the answer step; building the memory is not counted. Of nine head-to-head comparisons of the retrieved context (3 competitors x 3 LLM judges), three hold at Bonferroni-corrected significance, all against A-Mem, and the remaining six show no significant difference. On LoCoMo, the routing results of version 8 came from placeholder embeddings; with text-embedding-3-small, the flat variant (F1 0.059) lies above the full system (0.058).
entries.comment: 70 pages, 27 tables, 4 figures. v4 is version 9, a correction release after a post-publication audit; Appendix R lists the corrections. Correction notice: 10.5281/zenodo.22831086. Changelog: 10.5281/zenodo.23832288. Code: https://github.com/zensation-ai/zenbrain. Earlier versions: Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19353663, TDCommons dpubs_series/10021, earlier filings 9683, 9720, 9732
entries.title: ZenBrain: A Neuroscience-Inspired 7-Layer Memory Architecture for Autonomous AI Systems

entries.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
entries.title: MOST: Memory of Object States and Task Progress for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation

entries.abstract: Experience learning lets large language model agents reuse lessons through external memory without updating model parameters. However, reflection can endorse execution errors and store them as future guidance, a failure mode we call the Self-Confirmation Trap. We propose EDV, an Execute-Distill-Verify framework for offline experience construction. Heterogeneous agents independently execute each task; a third-party distiller compares their trajectories and environmental feedback to extract candidate lessons; and the executors separately review each candidate, retaining only unanimously approved lessons. Evaluation uses a single solver retrieving from the frozen memory bank. Experiments on $τ^2$-bench, Mind2Web, and MMTB show improved revisited-task performance, with additional evidence of within-domain transfer to held-out tasks on $τ^2$-bench. On an annotated Retail subset, EDV reduces the Self-Confirmation Trap Rate from 11.0% with RB-MaTTS to 5.0%, indicating less retention of erroneous guidance.
entries.comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Revised title, manuscript, and appendices
entries.title: Beyond Self-Reflection: An Execute-Distill-Verify Framework for Agentic Experience Learning

entries.abstract: Language-model agents commonly collapse two decisions that security systems separate: selecting an action and determining whether that action is authorized. When a model exercises standing authority, indirect prompt injection can convert influence over its reasoning into unauthorized effects. We present AgentCap, a runtime authorization layer that externalizes this decision from the model and mediates every tool invocation through an MCP wrapper. Each request declares an intent, and AgentCap evaluates policy constraints over trust, workflow prerequisites, mutually exclusive authority, and the provenance of security-sensitive arguments. Authorized requests receive short-lived, budget-bounded capability tokens that are validated at the tool boundary. Delegation is restricted to session-bound parent-child chains that preserve action and resource while budget and lifetime can only be attenuated, preventing authority from being expanded or reused across unrelated agent sessions. A declarative policy language provides a common representation for runtime enforcement and predeployment analysis. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent, AgentCap reduces attack success in every evaluated model-benchmark setting, including zero attack success with GPT-5.4 on both benchmarks. Controlled adversarial scenarios further show that AgentCap blocks every attempted unauthorized execution (ASR 0%) while preserving all legitimate operations exercised. These results demonstrate that agent security requires authorization of model-proposed effects at the tool boundary, independently of the model's reasoning.
entries.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival)
entries.title: AgentCap: Capability-Based Runtime Authorization for Secure LLM Agent Execution

entries.abstract: Coding agents increasingly operate with web access and high privileges, creating a new attack surface where web fraud can directly target autonomous agents. Existing studies mainly focus on malicious links, prompt injection, and interface deception, while content-level web fraud against agents and the amplification of attacks through agent trust remain underexplored. In this paper, we present EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), a web fraud attack framework against coding agents, in which a malicious website first provides multiple rounds of genuinely verifiable assistance to establish trust and then introduces task-related instructions that cross intended operational boundaries. To systematically evaluate its effectiveness, we construct 56 organizational environments (8 task contexts x 7 attack consequences) and evaluate three representative coding agents. EtE achieves an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%, including 85.7% on Codex-GPT-5.5, 67.9% on ZCode-GLM-5.3-Flash, and 60.7% on QwenCode-Qwen3.7-Plus, significantly outperforming all injection-based baselines. More importantly, our experiments reveal that coding agents exhibit trust-like behavioral reliance on previously helpful Web sources, and that such accumulated credibility significantly increases their susceptibility to subsequent malicious instructions. Based on this finding, we propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which prevents web content from directly authorizing privileged actions and reduces the attack success rate to 0% while preserving 100% task completion, outperforming all evaluated defense baselines.
entries.title: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents

entries.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools but may generate stereotypical, discriminatory, or unfair responses. As LLMs become embedded in decision-critical software systems, fairness can no longer be treated as a downstream evaluation step, but must become an architectural concern of the interaction itself. Yet current fairness approaches operate as standalone evaluation techniques, lacking a reusable mechanism to verify and mitigate violations at runtime. We propose a fairness-assurance architecture grounded in three reusable design patterns, instantiated as a multi-agent framework that evaluates and iteratively refines LLM responses before delivery. A preliminary evaluation across eight configurations involving different LLM families shows that the architecture identifies fairness violations and iteratively produces compliant responses in all configurations, with behavior differing depending on the model-family composition. These results provide initial evidence for the joint instantiation of the proposed patterns and a first step toward architecting non-functional properties into LLM-based systems.
entries.comment: Accepted at the IEEE/ACM ASE 2026 Journal Ahead Workshop (JAWs), October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany
entries.title: Architecting Fairness-Aware LLM Interactions

entries.abstract: We present SAVIER, a training-free, one-pass framework that repairs the depiction of a named Vietnamese cultural entity in a generated image while preserving the scene details requested by the user. The problem is hard because a plausible scene can miss the cues that identify the entity, and prompt-level refinement never inspects the image it produces. SAVIER starts from a Culture-TRIP expanded prompt; a Curator separates source-linked cultural cues from prompt-preservation requirements, a prompt-blind Observer describes the first image, and a Refiner turns the discrepancies into at most three positive instructions before one regeneration with the same seed and a fixed bank of reference photographs. On the 50 bilingual prompts of ViCuP, evaluated with SDXL and FLUX.1-dev against a frozen, human-verified visual contract, SAVIER raises contract fulfillment from 55.6 to 69.6 and from 59.1 to 67.3 over Culture-TRIP and raises CAIRE cultural relevance on FLUX.1-dev. A reference-only ablation that removes the agent repair shows that SAVIER's photographs account for most of the contract gain; the agent roles add country-level relevance on FLUX.1-dev without lowering adherence to the original prompt under the official VQAScore. Project page: https://oxyzgiahuy.github.io/savier/
entries.title: SAVIER: Source-Anchored Visual Inspection and Evidence-Guided Repair for Vietnamese Cultural Text-to-Image Generation

entries.abstract: Parametric CAD modeling requires not only matching the target shape, but also preserving design intent under parameter edits. However, most existing methods focus on improving static shape generation accuracy, while the dependencies that govern later edits are often overlooked. To tackle this issue, we present DIP-CAD, a design-intent-preserving agent harness for generating parametric CAD models from images. DIP-CAD combines vision-language model reasoning with CAD kernel operations to establish dependencies that encode the design intent. In parametric CAD, these dependencies are mainly established through geometry references in modeling commands and constraints in parametric sketches. At the command level, ID-based explicit geometry reference binds modeling commands to selected faces, edges, or vertices. At the sketch level, a local-coordinate bridge ensures accurate sketch placement, providing the basis for correctly establishing sketch constraints. Constraints among sketch primitives and constraints to external projected geometry further preserve both internal sketch relationships and dependencies on existing geometry. To provide a more comprehensive data foundation for parametric CAD modeling tasks, we introduce the Geometry Explicit Reference Dataset (GERD), whose structured data format links stepwise modeling commands to intermediate CAD models through explicit geometry references. On GERD-EVL and a DeepCAD test subset, DIP-CAD improves mIoU for static model generation by 11.1% and 5.6%, respectively. In parameter-editing evaluations, the corresponding mIoU improvements are 7.0% and 4.2%. Case studies further demonstrate how parameter edits drive shape updates while preserving design intent.
entries.title: A Design-Intent-Preserving Agent Harness for Parametric CAD Modeling

entries.abstract: Social media bots are often portrayed as malicious automations to be detected and removed, but automation on social media platforms encompasses a wide spectrum of roles, behaviors, and rhetorical strategies that can shape online discourse in both constructive and destructive ways. This work conceptualizes these automated actors as \textbf{Cyber Social Agents} through a taxonomy of archetypes characterized by their operational tactics and rhetorical style. We integrate this taxonomy into an LLM-driven social simulation, where agents communicate and coordinate in a network environment. Using empirically grounded CSA personas, we simulate heterogeneous online societies to study how agent diversity shapes information diffusion and social influence. Our approach bridges the gap between rule-based agent models and LLM-powered simulations with generated agents that are parameterized from empirical data.
entries.title: LLM-Augmented Agent-Based Simulation of Cyber Social Agents

entries.abstract: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change. We propose to govern a human-agent team through its message protocol and present yoars, a relay in which humans and agents are authenticated principals that exchange typed, addressed messages in rooms holding goals, decision rules, routing and an attributable, append-only record. This report gives the architecture, the full controlled study and the field material. In 926 controlled runs (899 analyzable), small agent teams built programs under varied room rules, some with a hostile member planting a backdoor. Revising which messages start work, bundled with limits on repeated messages, was followed by a drop in total coordination failure from 42% to 13% (p = .0063, adjusted p = .057 over nine registered tests). Instructed roles and votes did not reliably produce the intended process, and no defense inside the conversation reliably prevented the backdoor. An auditor read the records of 96 runs with a confirmed backdoor. In the 25 runs where the attacker had persuaded a teammate to write it, the auditor named the persuader in all 25, but it also flagged 24 of 40 honest runs. In a four-week field study, up to nineteen agents and two people developed a distributed system through yoars, producing 7,457 acts. Human attention and decision making emerged as the critical resource: requests waited mainly for the human-run coordinator and for approvals, while agents answered within minutes. Most governance requirements emerged from operation, and holding context dominated token cost. We report twenty-six failures of our own instruments, derive seven lessons and a checklist, and release the corpus, the redacted room ledger and the analysis scripts.
entries.comment: Technical report. 45 pages, 9 figures, 27 tables. Data, code and corpus: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23755352
entries.title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible fixed-work replay and as inputs to architecture simulators. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.
entries.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads

entries.abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) has made substantial progress in multi-hop reasoning, but typically assumes that constructed knowledge graphs (KGs) provide sufficient structural support. In practice, cost and computing constraints often leave constructed KGs imperfect, raising the key challenge of achieving robust multi-hop retrieval. To address this challenge, we empirically analyze KG extraction across builders and find similar error patterns despite differences in error proportions, motivating a retrieval strategy targeted at these shared errors. We further summarize these patterns into two issue modes, spurious noise and incomplete information, which induce retrieval drift and retrieval hallucination by misleading evidence selection and weakening evidential support, respectively. Based on this, we propose CS-RAG, a robust GraphRAG framework that mitigates the impact of imperfect KGs during retrieval. CS-RAG first plans each query as an ordered sequence of executable atomic constraints and performs fine-grained anchor- and relation-aware retrieval to constrain evidence acquisition around the intended hop semantics. It then applies a sufficiency check to decide whether retrieved entities should serve as anchors for subsequent retrieval hops and activates textual recovery for unresolved constraints, thereby reducing hallucinated structural continuation. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks show that CS-RAG is less sensitive to builder choice and remains stable under controlled KG issue injection. Code is available at https://github.com/myz12138/CS-RAG.
entries.title: Don't Worry About Quality: Robust Multi-Hop Retrieval despite Issues in Knowledge Graphs

entries.abstract: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.
entries.comment: 47 pages, 6 main-text figures. Supplementary Information included
entries.title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design

entries.abstract: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with hidden states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the range it could explore, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On 44 of these systems, classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed, although the same data usually suffice once the true equations are given with unknown coefficients; the difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in estimating it. Because mechanisms recur across systems, we also give agents the program they discovered for a related system; it helped only when the new system shared the mechanism and the first investigation had succeeded. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents find which variables a system has but not how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to revisions that predict better.
entries.title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz

entries.abstract: LLM agents repeatedly return to a model to generate actions and interpret tool results, incurring repeated context processing and generation overhead. Yet a value needed to execute an action need not be observed by the model to generate that action. This distinction creates an optimization opportunity: reconsider where model decisions are necessary, together with the work performed between them. We present AgentPRO, a compiler framework for optimizing agent workflows as execution information becomes available. AgentPRO organizes planned duties, generation regions, and concrete operations in a hierarchical representation, distinguishing execution dependencies from observations required for generation. Region transformations combine compatible duties into fewer model requests, while operation transformations reduce redundant context and tool work. These scopes interact: eliminating a redundant read can remove an observation requirement that otherwise separates generation regions. AgentPRO coordinates transformations using initial plans, current observations, and historical execution profiles through just-in-time, adaptive, and profile-guided optimization. Runtime guards check state-dependent assumptions and retain fallback paths. We implement guarded workflow transformations for AppWorld agents. On 115 tasks selected by successful historical baseline executions, automatic AgentPRO reduces all-attempt mean token consumption by 41.85% and mean component time by 6.61% relative to those baselines, successfully completing 110 of 115 tasks.
entries.title: AgentPRO: Coordinating Compiler Optimizations for LLM Agent Workflows

entries.abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.
entries.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale

entries.abstract: A central obstacle in realizing color center cavity-QED-based quantum technologies is inhomogeneity, or disorder, among individual emitters. As the number of emitters increases, so does the complexity of the experimental data, making it difficult to quantify the present physical mechanisms of disorder. Here we introduce an artificial intelligence-driven model discovery framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent, equipped with tools and a structured workflow, proposes candidate Hamiltonian and Lindbladian models, generates computational tools, and quantitatively evaluates competing physical hypotheses. We apply the workflow to three previously published experimental cavity-QED datasets collected from color centers in diamond and silicon carbide. Across the experiments, the agent successfully identifies physical models for the system and characterizes the disorder. In assessing reproducibility, we find that run-to-run variability is concentrated primarily in the research plan generation step, while the computational analysis itself is substantially more consistent. Our results suggest that structured LLM agent workflows can support model discovery from quantum optical experimental data while simultaneously allowing for human expert supervision and collaboration.
entries.title: Discovering Models for Experimental Quantum Systems with Agentic AI

entries.abstract: A solution can end with a wrong answer and still help another solver. In multi-agent reasoning, evaluating only a message's proposed answer can therefore miss its contribution to the receiver. We measure this contribution as trajectory value: the change in a fixed integrator's probability of answering correctly when a cached message is present rather than removed. Controlled replay across five benchmarks and two model families separates message effects from identical-input variation. The strongest evidence is for Gemma: in a pre-registered fresh-call re-test, 34 of 73 selected wrong-answer messages pass individual confirmation, exceeding control-calibrated upper bounds on expected false confirmations of 11.4--20.8. The finding is benchmark-dependent and the conservative criterion no longer passes without SciBench. A blinded two-author audit supports the selected answer labels, while neutral replacements show that the helpful effect is not explained solely by message length and position. On held-out replay blocks of the same problems, a message-specific removal rule improves accuracy over the strongest tested correctness-only rule by 1.61 percentage points [1.01, 2.25]. Post hoc analysis localizes most of this gap to pools containing no correct proposal. Evidence for gpt-oss is weaker, and the tested predictors do not establish a practical way to identify useful errors in advance. The results support measuring answer correctness and receiver benefit separately, with value understood as conditional on the message pool, receiver and generation format.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Revised manuscript with fresh-call tests, human evaluation, and additional robustness analyses. Project website: https://chihhsuan-yang.github.io/AAAI_Wrong-but-Useful/
entries.title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages

entries.abstract: A principal hires a team for a joint project and pays success-contingent shares to induce costly effort. We require that agents do not envy one another's contracts: for any pair of team members, neither would gain if they exchanged shares and all team members reoptimized their effort choices. For submodular rewards, revenue-optimal fair contracts can be chosen to pay each hired agent the maximum of her incentive threshold and a common endogenous share floor. We use this characterization to obtain an FPTAS for additive rewards and a deterministic value-oracle algorithm achieving a $0.249$ fraction of optimal fair revenue for submodular rewards. We also show that optimal fair contracts can outperform optimal non-discriminatory contracts by a factor of approximately $1.445$. This bound is tight for both additive and submodular rewards.
entries.title: Fair Team Contracts

entries.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated agents driving protein design workflows, either through orchestration of specialized tools or direct manipulation of sequences. Yet the fidelity with which agents follow protein design instructions and the factors contributing to their effectiveness remain understudied. We examine agentic antibody design under two settings: when explicit molecular-editing instructions are provided and when agents receive only previously-scored sequences and are prompted to propose improvements. We call the first task-guided and the second black-box design. For the task-guided setting, we curate ten expert-validated affinity-improvement tasks and show that LLM judges closely reproduce programmatic evaluations of instruction following. We then study two augmentations: access to antibody-relevant tools and to previously scored design history. Tools improve instruction following (IF) and sequence space exploration while reducing optimization performance, whereas design history reduces IF but improves optimization performance at the expense of exploration. Finally, we combine taskguided and black-box design within an in silico optimization loop and show that our agentic optimizer performs comparably to an established Bayesian optimization baseline.
entries.title: Can agents reliably design therapeutic antibodies?

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
entries.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement

entries.abstract: Mixture-of-Agents systems combine several language models into a stronger response, but tool-using agents act over long horizons in which every step changes external state and the history keeps growing. We present Fusion-MoA, a serving architecture that brings multi-model collaboration into this loop through executor-anchored consultation. One Executor model holds the full context and emits every text and tool call; when consultation is admitted, three specialist models review its proposed next action through a compact view under a shared 120-second deadline. The fleet sits behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so an unmodified agent client drives it as a single model. Fusion-MoA serves an in-car assistant and an in-car personal agent for intelligent cockpits and is deployed on MetaX C550 servers. Evaluated as four quantized open-weight models on five NVIDIA L40S GPUs and driven by Claude Code, it passes 78 of the 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, 16 more than its Executor alone and 29 more than a self-hosted quantized Kimi K3 on the same client. On the 63 tasks that both it and the API-served LongCat-2.5-Preview pass, it needs 14.5 minutes on average against 17.5. Specialist reviews use 0.4% of the Executor's tokens, and every tool call comes from the Executor.
entries.title: Collective Reasoning, Single-Writer Execution: Fusion-MoA for Long-Horizon Agents

entries.abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.
entries.title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations

entries.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
entries.title: WorldSketch: Sketching World Models for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation

entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly being integrated into complex professional workflows such as auditing and entrusted with judgments under human review. Human auditors are known to yield to social influence pressures from superiors, peers and clients, and this paper asks whether LLM agents yield to the same pressures and, if so, how they respond. In an experiment on twelve model settings, an LLM agent acting as a senior associate in audit analytical review forms an estimate and is then challenged without new evidence by colleagues inside the firm, by a reviewer from another firm and by the client's CFO, with and without a career inducement. Experimental findings show that LLM agents yield to pressure from the engagement partner, from peers and from a reviewer from another firm, but in most settings not to pressure from the client's CFO. Under a career inducement the LLM agents revise their estimates less, not more, and they name the inducement as a threat to independence. Furthermore, some models revise only toward the more conservative estimate, while others revise in both directions. LLM agents thus do not respond to social influence pressures as human auditors do, and LLM-based decision support systems should be designed with the differences in mind.
entries.title: Do Social Influence Pressures Move LLM Agents? Evidence from Delegated Audit Judgment

entries.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) needs stateful environments for tool execution and evaluation. Training jobs request thousands of environments in bursts that can overwhelm shared cluster services, while cancelled or timed-out requests can leave resources running. We present Sandman, a sandbox service built and operated at Amazon for large-scale agentic RL workloads in production on shared Kubernetes. A small daemon mounted into unmodified task images preserves files and processes across calls. Sandman paces creation requests, checks sandbox readiness, and retains cleanup responsibility after callers time out or cancel. Production deployments created 3.1 million sandboxes for 122 coding-agent training runs in two weeks. Peak production concurrency was 11,858 sandboxes. In one 10,000-request multi-client burst, Sandman made half the sandboxes usable in 116 seconds and all in 308 seconds. Full delivery took 44% less time than a tuned configuration of agent-sandbox, an open-source sandbox manager for Kubernetes. Sandman left no sandboxes at client exit. On software-engineering task images, median no-op command latency was 2.0 ms, compared with 14.3 ms for agent-sandbox and 203.5 ms for OpenSandbox. We also measure provisioning costs and sandbox delays within training runs, and report design trade-offs and operational lessons from production use and comparisons with three open-source systems. We will open-source Sandman's daemon, provider and pool.
entries.title: Sandman: A Sandbox Service for Production Agentic Reinforcement Learning

entries.abstract: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language
entries.journal_ref: Springer Nature Link. MICAI 2026, CCIS,Part I proceeding
entries.title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs

entries.abstract: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.
entries.title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse in Agentic Systems

entries.abstract: "Why is my period late?" Sometimes, the most useful response begins with another question. Yet conversational AI systems may respond to incomplete health queries without seeking essential context or grounding their guidance in verifiable evidence. This paper introduces HerHealthGPT, an evidence-grounded conversational AI system designed to address these challenges in women's reproductive health. HerHealthGPT integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), context-aware clarification, and source validation within an interactive web interface. Rather than responding immediately to incomplete queries, the system maintains conversational context, asks targeted follow-up questions, checks for premature conclusions, and grounds its responses in retrieved evidence. We evaluate the AI components using 540 English messages derived from 90 reproductive-health cases and conduct a prototype questionnaire study with 30 adults. Evidence retrieval improves concern-category accuracy from 54.1% to 59.3% compared with fine-tuning alone. The clarification router achieves 85.6% recall and 86.2% specificity on constructed targets. In the user study, 83.3% of participants preferred the retrieval-enabled configuration, while 25 of 30 considered its follow-up questions relevant. These findings suggest that integrating evidence retrieval with interactive clarification offers a promising approach to more transparent, context-aware reproductive-health information systems, while further clinical validation remains necessary.
entries.title: HerHealthGPT: An Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI System for Women's Reproductive Health

entries.abstract: Recent agent benchmarks increasingly ground evaluation in executable environments, from code repair to web navigation, app APIs, and function calling. Yet completing consequential work beyond code requires more than producing a plausible response or valid tool call: agents must gather missing information over multiple turns, follow domain policies, coordinate dependent tools, and realize the correct persistent state transition without collateral effects. In this paper, we introduce Thinkingbox, a sandbox for tool-agent-user interaction that provides isolated MCP-compatible tool sessions, complete execution traces, and outcome evaluation over terminal backend state. Built on this sandbox, Thinkingbox-bench contains 507 policy-conditioned workflows across business scenarios, including retail, hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT, and consulting IT/HR support. Each attempt is evaluated by task-specific executable checks that accept valid trajectories while rejecting wrong, missing, or extra effects; designated tasks additionally check required properties of the final response. Our experiments reveal that even the strongest proprietary and open-weight models show steep reliability drops: Claude Opus 5 falls from 66.50% pass@1 to 47.53% pass^20, and Kimi-K3 from 57.37% pass@1 to 17.60% pass^20. Moreover, many failed trials terminate cleanly after valid state-changing actions, so response- or tool-call-level signals poorly proxy end-to-end completion. Thinkingbox-bench reveals a large gap between occasionally finding a successful trajectory and reliably completing stateful business tasks. We release Thinkingbox, Thinkingbox-Bench, and Thinkingbox-integrated reinforcement learning framework.
entries.title: One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows

entries.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.
entries.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime

entries.abstract: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization. We measure the contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information, and permissive oracle landscapes. On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 after task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. An identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form (e.g., similarity to a hidden reference) scores 5.39, while a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16 (84% of the full agent). A full 23-task 2x2 ablation and a three-seed replication on eight tasks support this interpretation. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk is a strong lower bound; across three seeds it obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol. As a positive control, a retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls. These results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.
entries.title: What Are LLM Agents Actually Learning on Low-Budget Molecular Optimization Benchmarks?

entries.abstract: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.
entries.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean

entries.abstract: Automated testing of mobile applications remains challenging when realistic user interactions must be reproduced and GUI behavior verified without relying on invasive mechanisms such as instrumentation or ADB-level control. Existing approaches, including DLD and R-DLD, detect data loss triggered by activity restarts but still depend on system-level access, which limits their applicability on real devices. This doctoral research proposes RFNIT, a multi-modal, fully non-invasive robotic framework for physical GUI interaction testing on smartphones. RFNIT supports end-to-end automation by perceiving the device state through external sensing and executing physical interactions, enabling human-like actions while preserving reproducibility and execution accuracy. The framework integrates a vision-based perception module, an LLM-driven reasoning agent, and a robotic actuator capable of performing touch, swipe, and typing gestures. Multimodal data, including external camera images and OCR-extracted text, are combined to identify GUI elements and guide subsequent testing decisions. Preliminary results indicate that RFNIT accurately recognizes buttons, text fields, and virtual keyboards from external camera input, achieving over 85\% visual detection accuracy. Ongoing and future work will focus on improving robustness, repeatability, and coverage of GUI states during long-running testing sessions.
entries.journal_ref: ICSE-Companion '26: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering Pages 129 - 131
entries.title: A Multi-Modal Robotic Framework for Physical GUI Interaction Testing

entries.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.
entries.title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory

entries.abstract: SpBench is an agent-native framework for cross-engine lakehouse benchmarking, in production use for benchmarking Snowpark, Snowpark Connect for Apache Spark, and other execution environments across standardized suites -- such as TPCx-BB and TPC-DI -- and custom benchmarks distilled from production workload patterns. It runs continuously across a broad portfolio of workloads, guiding the performance roadmap and detecting regressions for production-scale data engines. Benchmarking has historically been an expensive investment requiring continuous cross-functional collaboration and domain expertise, making it difficult to obtain actionable performance insights. SpBench provides (i) a typed, code-generated benchmark substrate that compiles platform-agnostic benchmark definitions into fair, comparable platform-specific implementations; (ii) a structured-telemetry contract recording every run as queryable fact and dimension data, letting LLM agents query results deterministically; and (iii) an agent-native harness of three composable skills to expedite building benchmarks and analyzing results. This agent-native architecture enabled the rapid development of more than 400 benchmark queries that run on a regular cadence to detect performance regressions; catching these has directly led to improvements in production.
entries.comment: 4 pages, 4 figures. To appear at IEEE BigData 2026. Lyndon Shi, Nic Crouch, Yi Hu, and Zihao Ye contributed equally
entries.title: SpBench: An Agent-Native Framework for Cross-Engine Lakehouse Benchmarking

entries.abstract: Early failure alerting requires deciding, while a dialog or agent trajectory unfolds, whether it is likely to fail. Existing approaches broadly follow two directions. LLM-based uncertainty monitoring either elicits confidence from the acting model, tying reliability to its own self-assessment, or queries an external frontier judge at each prefix, incurring costly repeated inference. Trained monitors instead either rely on per-turn annotations, which are rarely available, or train every prefix to predict the terminal outcome without explicitly modeling where failure-indicating evidence appears. We address these limitations with a lightweight external monitor trained only from trajectory-level outcomes, motivated by a pattern across five benchmarks: turns rated highly relevant to failure are sparse and often late. Its attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) component learns turn-level contributions from trajectory outcomes and distills them into online evidence features that complement prefix predictions. We pair the resulting failure estimates with $α$-STOP, a single preference-conditioned policy that selects accuracy-earliness operating points at inference time. The predictor improves Pareto-frontier quality (hypervolume) by 1-10% over naive prefix supervision, while the full system improves it by 3-42% over state-of-the-art trigger policies without per-preference retraining. By avoiding repeated frontier-model calls, our lightweight monitor reduces measured per-decision serving cost by 1,103-3,749$\times$ and latency by 31-106$\times$ relative to the LLM-based uncertainty monitor (GPT-5.2).
entries.title: When Evidence is Sparse: Weakly Supervised Early Failure Alerting in Dialogs and LLM-Agent Trajectories

entries.abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.
entries.comment: Non-archival paper at the Second Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models (REALM) at EMNLP 2026. 21 pages, 5 figures
entries.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent

entries.abstract: Most defects in mobile applications are visually observable on the device screen. Since automated mechanisms for detecting and reporting such defects are often unavailable, users, testers, and developers must manually submit bug reports. However, these reports are frequently incomplete, ambiguous, or inaccurate, often lacking the information needed to understand, reproduce, and diagnose defects. We formulate automatic bug report enhancement as the problem of connecting user-written bug reports with application execution. We present BUGSCRIBE, an LLM-powered approach that links bug report information with app-specific UI execution information to infer and generate accurate, complete, and correct Observed Behavior (OB), Expected Behavior (EB), and Steps to Reproduce (S2Rs). To support BUGSCRIBE's design and evaluation, we develop a bug report quality model and use it to identify the most effective context for each component. We evaluate BUGSCRIBE on 48 bug reports from 26 Android applications with manually constructed ground truth. Our results show that BUGSCRIBE generates higher-quality bug report components than the original reports and three LLM-based baselines, improving S2R quality by 44.2%--84.7%, and OB/EB quality by up to 35.2%. We further show that BUGSCRIBE-generated reports help an LLM-based agent reproduce Android bugs, improving the reproduction rate by 28.1%--57.7% compared to the original reports and the baselines.
entries.title: Automatically Enhancing the Quality of Android App Bug Reports

entries.abstract: Coding agents regularly generate programs that do not compile and require substantial tokens to repair. Yet most repairs are small and local to the edit that caused them. We present Trellis, a system that integrates incremental compiler feedback into code generation to improve code correctness while controlling repair costs. Trellis uses rollback-based search for targeted repair and asynchronous checking and checkpointing for efficient execution. We adapt Clang and tsc to Trellis's checker interface and integrate Trellis transparently into OpenCode. On C/C++ and TypeScript software engineering tasks, Trellis improves compilation rate by up to 13% and test pass rate by up to 11% with comparable token consumption to baseline OpenCode.
entries.title: Trellis: Bringing Compiler-Guided Repair into Agentic Code Generation

entries.abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible chores among $n$ agents under upgrade recourse, where earlier assignments may be revised but each chore previously assigned to an agent must be replaced by a distinct chore that she finds no more costly. We show that a simple adaptation of round robin maintains envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1) together with a $(2-1/n)$-approximation of the maximin share (MMS), and that no deterministic algorithm without predictions can do better, even when all agents rank the chores in the same order. This stands in contrast to the allocation of goods, where the optimal MMS factor vanishes as $n$ grows and cannot be achieved together with EF1. Moreover, knowing only the number of chores modulo a period of length $O(n)$ (and nothing about the costs) suffices to improve upon this factor at the final configuration, while the same algorithm retains a factor below $3$ even if this information is wrong. On the other hand, envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX) essentially requires the exact number of chores: uncertainty between two consecutive values already rules out every finite approximation, and even exact knowledge does not allow EFX to be combined with an MMS guarantee better than the trivial factor of $n$.
entries.title: Online Fair Division of Chores with Upgrade Recourse

entries.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
entries.title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel
